title: Does a predictive gap-seeking planner recover the framing a follow camera loses when it avoids pedestrians?
summary: capture-follow found that a repulsion-field controller trades framing for distance: at 0.1 people/m² a drone that ignores pedestrians frames 99.8% of the time with 523 contacts (within 0.5 m) per hour, and 67.8% with 161 once it avoids them. Here a sampler that predicts pedestrians 3 s ahead and picks a velocity that goes round and rejoins is run on the same crowds (8 seeds). Framing is not recovered at equal settings: the planner at a 1.5 m radius frames the drone 58.0% of the time (repulsion 67.8%) but with 36 contacts an hour, not 161. What it changes is the trade-off: on the drone’s framing-against-contacts curve the planner sits to the left of repulsion (89% framed at 281 contacts against 79% at 322; 58% at 36 against 58.5% at 92), and on ground platforms at 0.1 people/m² it cuts contacts from 326 to 21 (wheeled, flat plaza) with the same 40% framing. At 0.3 people/m² both controllers lose the frame (3 to 39%). Pedestrians ignore the platform and their velocities are known exactly, so the planner is an upper bound on perception. Platform figures are capture-follow’s assumed round numbers, not datasheets.
lede: does a predictive planner recover the framing a follow camera loses by avoiding pedestrians? Not at equal settings (drone 58% framed vs 68% for repulsion at 0.1 people/m²), but it halves-to-tenths the contacts (36 vs 161 per hour; wheeled 21 vs 326) and moves the framing/contacts front left. 2-D simulation, assumed platform figures.
